title: Planet Hunters
sub: Grades 5–8 Science · Another Earth · Finding planets we cannot see
objective: Students will learn how astronomers find planets around other stars without seeing them: by the tiny dip in a star’s light as a planet passes in front of it, or by the star’s wobble as the planet tugs on it. They will model a transit, read light curves, and weigh what the evidence about HD 20794 d shows, and what it cannot yet tell us.

objectives.heading: By the end of this lesson you will be able to:
objectives.why: Most of what astronomers know about other worlds comes from clues in starlight, not from pictures. Reading indirect evidence well is one of the most useful skills in science.

items.text: explain the two clues astronomers use to find planets they cannot see: a dip in a star’s light, and a star’s wobble
items.question: explain the two clues astronomers use to find hidden planets?

items.text: read a light curve to find when a planet passes its star, and how long its year is
items.question: read a light curve to find a planet’s year?

items.text: describe a habitable zone, and use the facts about HD 20794 d to say what we know and do not know about it
items.question: say what we know, and do not know, about HD 20794 d?

items.text: judge a claim about another Earth, weighing evidence for it, against it, and still missing
items.question: judge a claim about another Earth, using evidence for, against and missing?

materials: A lamp with a bare bulb or a strong flashlight (the star); a small ball on a stick or string (the planet)
Optional: a phone with a light-meter app, held facing the lamp, to show the dip as a number
Page 3 of this plan, projected or printed; differentiated handouts, one per student
connection: **On the poster** *Another Earth*, find *How do you find a planet you can’t see?* and the paragraphs about Kepler, HD 20794 d and Webb. Next, the poster asks why we have not found aliens yet.

steps.title: A planet you can’t see
script: Show the poster’s alien world. Ask its own question: *“How do you find a planet you can’t see?”* A star is so bright, and its planets so small and far, that the planet is lost in the glare. Then turn on the lamp and darken the room: *“This is a star. Somewhere near it is a planet. Watch the light.”* Pass the ball between the lamp and the class, slowly.

screen.alt: The poster’s alien world: purple cliffs and three moons in a violet sky
screen.caption: How do you find a planet you can’t see?

steps.purpose: Pose the puzzle before giving the answer.
students: Planets around other stars are hidden in their star’s glare.
How could you know a planet is there?

steps.title: Two clues
script: **Two clues.** Read the poster: *“Planets are hidden in the glare of their stars, so astronomers usually hunt for clues instead. They watch for tiny dips in a star’s light when a planet passes in front of it, or for a star’s wobble as an orbiting planet tugs on it.”* The ball made the lamp dim a little: that is a **transit**, and a graph of a star’s brightness over time is a **light curve**. A planet and its star tug on each other, so the star moves in a small circle: its **wobble**.

screen.text: Planets are hidden in the glare of their stars, so astronomers usually hunt for clues instead. They watch for tiny dips in a star’s light when a planet passes in front of it, or for a star’s wobble as an orbiting planet tugs on it.
screen.cite: Another Earth · How do you find a planet you can’t see?

steps.purpose: Name the transit and the wobble, and see each in the model.
students: What happened to the light when the ball passed?
Why would a planet make its star wobble?

steps.title: Thousands of planets
script: **The search.** In 1992 the first exoplanets were found; in 1995, the first around a star like our Sun. Play the launch: NASA’s Kepler telescope, launched in 2009, found more than 2,600 planets by watching for dips. Today over 6,000 are confirmed.

screen.question: Kepler watched for dips in starlight. What did it find?

steps.purpose: See how far the search has come, from the first finds to over 6,000.
students: The first exoplanets were found in 1992.
Kepler found more than 2,600. How many are confirmed today?

steps.title: A super-Earth
script: **A super-Earth.** HD 20794 d is about 20 light-years away, roughly six times Earth’s mass, in its star’s **habitable zone**: where temperatures could allow liquid water. Its year lasts about 647 days, on a stretched oval orbit that swings between the zone’s inner and outer edges. It took more than 20 years of measurements to confirm it, in 2025. Webb can now read starlight that filters through a planet’s air.

screen.text: Since then, over 6,000 exoplanets have been confirmed, including HD 20794 d, a “super-Earth” located about 20 light-years away in the constellation Eridanus. This planet is roughly six times the mass of Earth and orbits within its star’s habitable zone, where temperatures could allow liquid water to exist. HD 20794 d takes about 647 days to circle its star. Its orbit is a stretched oval, so over its year it swings between the inner and outer edges of the habitable zone. Astronomers confirmed it in 2025, using more than 20 years of measurements.

steps.purpose: Meet HD 20794 d, and the habitable zone.
students: Does HD 20794 d stay inside it all year?

steps.title: Transit lab
script: In groups or as a class, test two questions with the lamp. A larger ball blocks more light: a deeper dip. A ball that passes above or below the lamp, from where the class sits, makes no dip at all, so a transit is seen only when a planet’s orbit lines up with our view.

screen.question: Does a bigger planet make a bigger dip? What if its orbit doesn’t pass in front of the star?

steps.purpose: Test the model: what changes the dip, and when there is no dip at all.
students: Try a small ball, then a large one.
Now pass the ball above the lamp, not in front. What do you see?

steps.title: Choose a handout
script: Students then choose a handout. Every light curve on them is **practice data, made up for the worksheet**, and labeled so.

levels.name: Green Level
levels.summary: Match each clue to what it tells us. Read a practice light curve: circle the dips and count the days between them. Fill in a card about HD 20794 d from a word bank.

levels.name: Yellow Level
levels.summary: Explain both methods. Read a light curve to find a planet’s year. Compare HD 20794 d’s year with Earth’s. Weigh the claim *HD 20794 d is another Earth.*

levels.name: Red Level
levels.summary: Untangle a light curve with two planets in it. Explain why most planets never transit from our view. Use Kepler’s estimate. Judge the claim, naming evidence for, against and still missing.

steps.purpose: Read light curves and weigh the evidence, at the right level of challenge.
students: Choose Green, Yellow or Red. All three read a light curve and HD 20794 d.

steps.title: Look back
script: Ask the objectives back as questions, from the screen or page 1: *“Can you now…?”* Students show a thumb up, sideways or down.

steps.title: Clues left behind
script: Close with the poster’s question about clues, on the screen. Take three answers.

screen.question: Astronomers often find planets from the clues they leave rather than by seeing them. What else do we know about only from the clues it leaves behind?

steps.purpose: Carry the idea of indirect evidence beyond astronomy.
students: Think of one thing we know only from its clues.
